messages.text: 你好，我想請問一下這篇論文在講什麼？我對遊戲設計有興趣，但是英文不是我的母語，所以想先大概了解一下。

messages.short_answer: 這篇論文提出 MDA 框架（Mechanics 機制、Dynamics 動態、Aesthetics 美學），作為理解與設計遊戲的正式方法，希望幫助遊戲設計、遊戲評論與技術遊戲研究之間的溝通與迭代流程。

sections.title: MDA 三個組成部分的定義
sections.text: 論文把遊戲拆成三個部分：Mechanics 指遊戲的具體元件，位於資料表示與演算法層次；Dynamics 指機制在執行時，面對玩家輸入與彼此輸出後產生的行為；Aesthetics 指玩家與遊戲系統互動時，被引發的期望情緒反應。

sections.title: 三者如何互相連動
sections.text: 可以把 MDA 想成三個看遊戲的「透鏡」。從設計者角度，機制產生動態系統行為，進而帶來特定的美學體驗；從玩家角度，美學先定下調性，再體現在可觀察的動態中，最後回到可操作的機制。

sections.title: 論文的目的與背景
sections.text: 作者認為遊戲與書籍、音樂、電影不同，因為玩家的消費過程比較不可預測。論文希望 MDA 能橫跨遊戲設計與開發、遊戲評論，以及技術遊戲研究，讓不同領域的人都能拆解、研究並設計遊戲。

sections.title: 論文中的應用例子
sections.text: 概覽顯示，論文以 Monopoly（大富翁）為例，說明回饋循環如何拉大玩家差距，並提出補貼落後者、對領先者加稅等調整；也以 AI 追逐遊戲原型，說明目標受眾與美學目標如何改變設計需求。這些是概覽的摘要，不是原文逐字內容。

sources.text: In this paper we present the MDA framework (standing for Mechanics, Dynamics, and Aesthetics), developed and taught as part of the Game Design and Tuning Workshop at the Game Developers Conference, San Jose 2001-2004 [LeBlanc, 2004a]. MDA is a formal approach to understanding games – one which attempts to bridge the gap between game design and development, game criticism, and technical game research. We believe this methodology will clarify and strengthen the iterative processes of developers, scholars and researchers alike, making it easier for all parties to decompose, study and design a broad class of game designs and game artifacts. Towards a Comprehensive Framework Game design and authorship happen at many levels, and the fields of games research and development involve people from diverse creative and scholarly backgrounds. While it’s often necessary to focus on one area, everyone, regardless of discipline, will at some point need to consider issues outside that area: base mechanisms of game systems, the overarching design goals, or the desired experiential results of gameplay.
quotes: MDA is a formal approach to understanding games – one which attempts to bridge the gap between game design and development, game criticism, and technical game research.

sources.text:
The difference between games and other entertainment products (such as books, music, movies and plays) is that their consumption is relatively unpredictable. The string of events that occur during gameplay and the outcome of those events are unknown at the time the product is finished.

The MDA framework formalizes the consumption of games by breaking them into their distinct components:

...and establishing their design counterparts:

Mechanics describes the particular components of the game, at the level of data representation and algorithms.

Dynamics describes the run-time behavior of the mechanics acting on player inputs and each others’ outputs over time.

Aesthetics describes the desirable emotional responses evoked in the player, when she interacts with the game system.

Fundamental to this framework is the idea that games are more like artifacts than media. By this we mean that the content of a game is its behavior – not the media that streams out of it towards the player.
quotes: Mechanics describes the particular components of the game, at the level of data representation and algorithms.

sources.text:
Thinking about games as designed artifacts helps frame them as systems that build behavior via interaction. It supports clearer design choices and analysis at all levels of study and development. MDA in Detail MDA as Lens Each component of the MDA framework can be thought of as a “lens” or a “view” of the game – separate, but causally linked. [LeBlanc, 2004b].

From the designer’s perspective, the mechanics give rise to dynamic system behavior, which in turn leads to particular aesthetic experiences. From the player’s perspective, aesthetics set the tone, which is born out in observable dynamics and eventually, operable mechanics.

When working with games, it is helpful to consider both the designer and player perspectives. It helps us observe how even small changes in one layer can cascade into others. In addition, thinking about the player encourages experience-driven (as opposed to feature-driven) design.
quotes: From the designer’s perspective, the mechanics give rise to dynamic system behavior, which in turn leads to particular aesthetic experiences.

sources.text: These pages introduce the MDA framework (Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics) for analysing and designing games, contrasting games with other entertainment products because their consumption is unpredictable. The framework treats games as artifacts whose content is their behavior, and defines Mechanics as data representations and algorithms, Dynamics as run-time behavior, and Aesthetics as desired emotional responses. Each component is presented as a lens causally linked to the others, with designer and player perspectives explained and experience-driven design favored over feature-driven design. The pages then move to a taxonomy of eight aesthetic categories (Sensation, Fantasy, Narrative, Challenge, Fellowship, Discovery, Expression, Submission), illustrated with examples of Charades, Quake, The Sims and Final Fantasy, and note there is no formula for what produces fun.

These pages introduce a taxonomy-based approach to describing games, using aesthetics, dynamics, and mechanics as a framework for understanding player appeal. They present aesthetic models, illustrated with competitive games like Charades and Quake, which rely on adversarial play and clear feedback about who is winning. The dynamics section explains how elements such as time pressure, information sharing, item building, and rising tension produce experiences like challenge, fellowship, expression, and dramatic tension. Using Monopoly as the main example, the pages describe how feedback loops can widen gaps between players and erode engagement, and suggest design fixes such as catch-up rewards. The pages do not state formal limitations beyond noting that realism may conflict with fun.

These pages discuss how game designers can adjust game mechanics to shape overall dynamics, using Monopoly as a running example: adding subsidies and taxes to keep lagging players competitive, adding time-pressure mechanics such as constant-rate taxes or doubled payouts, and iteratively play-testing and tuning values until the game is balanced. They note that aesthetic vocabulary and dynamic models (such as the D6 model for board size) help designers articulate goals, diagnose problems, and measure progress. The pages then argue that AI components cannot be treated as black boxes and must be evaluated for their effects on system behavior and player experience. Using a baby-sitting tag game prototyped across three passes (for 3-7 year-olds, for 7-12 year-old girls with a Rugrats-style franchise, and as a strategic military simulation for 14-35 year old men), the pages show how target audience and aesthetic goals change design requirements for dynamics, hiding places, and character behaviour.

messages.text: 好，我大概懂一點了。那 Mechanics、Dynamics、Aesthetics 這三個分別是什麼意思？可以用簡單一點的方式解釋嗎？我英文不太好，想確認自己的理解。

messages.short_answer: 簡單來說：Mechanics 是遊戲的組成零件（規則、資料與演算法）；Dynamics 是這些零件在遊戲執行時、與玩家輸入及彼此互動後產生的行為；Aesthetics 是玩家在與遊戲互動時所產生的情感反應。

sections.title: 三個詞的白話解釋
sections.text: 可以把 Mechanics 想成「遊戲的零件與規則」，Dynamics 想成「遊戲開始跑之後，這些零件怎麼互相作用、隨時間產生的變化」，Aesthetics 則是「玩家玩的時候心裡的感受，例如好玩、緊張、有成就感」。

sections.title: 論文原文的定義
sections.text: 論文對 Mechanics 的描述是遊戲的特定組成部分，位於資料表示與演算法的層級；Dynamics 是機制在執行時，作用於玩家輸入與彼此輸出、隨時間的行為；Aesthetics 是玩家與遊戲系統互動時，被引發的期望情感反應。

sections.title: 用例子幫助理解
sections.text: 以一款跳躍遊戲為例（這是說明用的假設例子，並非論文內容）：Mechanics 可能是「按下跳躍鍵角色會跳起、重力會把角色拉下」；Dynamics 是玩家連續跳躍躲避障礙時，節奏與難度隨時間逐漸形成的情況；Aesthetics 則可能是玩家感到的緊張與挑戰感。

sections.title: 三者的關係與方向
sections.text: 論文指出三者是彼此分開、但有因果連結的「透鏡」。從設計者角度看，機制產生動態行為，動態再帶出美學體驗；從玩家角度看，美學設定基調，並體現在可觀察的動態與最終可操作的機制中。

messages.text: 所以我的理解是：Dynamics 就是設計者寫下來的規則，像是「按跳躍鍵角色會跳起」那種，而 Mechanics 是玩家在遊戲裡實際看到的行為，例如連續跳躍時節奏慢慢形成。這樣對嗎？

messages.short_answer: 你的理解前後有點顛倒。依論文定義，Mechanics 是遊戲的組成零件（資料表示與演算法層級的規則與結構）；Dynamics 則是這些機制在遊戲執行時，受玩家輸入與彼此輸出影響、隨時間產生的行為。所以「按跳躍鍵角色會跳起」比較接近 Mechanics，「連續跳躍時節奏慢慢形成」比較接近 Dynamics。

sections.title: 論文原文的定義
sections.text: 論文對 Mechanics 的描述是遊戲的特定組成部分，位於資料表示與演算法的層級；對 Dynamics 的描述則是機制在執行時的行為，會受玩家輸入以及彼此的輸出影響，並隨時間展開。兩者的差別在於一個是「零件」，一個是「零件運作起來之後的行為」。

sections.title: 用白話記住兩者的差別
sections.text: 可以把 Mechanics 想成遊戲的「零件和規則」，例如跳躍按鍵對應到跳起這條規則；把 Dynamics 想成「這些零件開始運轉、彼此碰撞後，玩家實際感受到的過程」，例如很多次跳躍之後形成的節奏。前者是靜態的設計內容，後者是執行時才出現的行為。

sections.title: 論文中卡牌遊戲的例子
sections.text: 論文以卡牌遊戲為例：洗牌、吃墩與下注等機制，可能讓「虛張聲勢（bluffing）」這種動態出現。這個例子說明機制是先存在的組成部分，而動態是玩家在遊戲中互動後才浮現的行為。（此例子為論文原文提到的內容，下方的跳躍例子則是為了幫助理解而自行舉的示意。）

sources.text:
For example, the mechanics of card games include shuffling, trick-taking and betting – from which dynamics like bluffing can emerge. The mechanics of shooters include weapons, ammunition and spawn points – which sometimes produce things like camping and sniping. The mechanics of golf include balls, clubs, sand traps and water hazards – which sometimes produce broken or drowned clubs.

Adjusting the mechanics of a game helps us fine-tune the game’s overall dynamics. Consider our Monopoly example. Mechanics that would help lagging players could include bonuses or “subsidies” for poor players, and penalties or “taxes” for rich players – perhaps calculated when crossing the Go square, leaving jail, or exercising monopolies over a certain threshold in value. By applying such changes to the fundamental rules of play, we might be able to keep lagging players competitive and interested for longer periods of time.
quotes: For example, the mechanics of card games include shuffling, trick-taking and betting – from which dynamics like bluffing can emerge.

messages.short_answer: 可以用一個簡單的區分來想：Mechanics 是設計者放進遊戲裡的「零件」（規則與結構），Dynamics 是這些零件在遊戲進行時，跟玩家操作和彼此互動後，「一段時間內反覆出現的行為模式」。前者是你能直接指出來的規則，後者是你在玩的過程中觀察到的結果。

sections.title: 用你玩的遊戲來區分
sections.text: 以射擊遊戲為例：子彈數量、重生點、武器種類都是 Mechanics，因為它們是設計者寫進遊戲的東西。玩家為了不被發現而躲在草叢或角落等待敵人，這種「反覆出現的走位與埋伏」則比較像 Dynamics，因為它是規則跟玩家操作一起運作後才慢慢出現的行為。（這是我舉的例子，不是論文中的內容。）

sections.title: 一個判斷問題
sections.text: 你可以問自己兩個問題：「這是設計者明確定下的規則或結構嗎？」如果是，較接近 Mechanics。「這是玩家在多次遊玩中，因為規則互相作用而反覆看到的行為模式嗎？」如果是，較接近 Dynamics。論文也用卡牌遊戲說明：洗牌、吃牌、下注是機制，從中可能浮現「虛張聲勢」這種動態。

messages.text: 我平常玩《英雄聯盟》，裡面每個英雄都有自己的技能冷卻時間，還有擊殺後會拿到金錢可以買裝備。我想問：冷卻時間和買裝備這些，是屬於 Mechanics、Dynamics，還是 Aesthetics 呢？我還是有點分不清楚，可以用我的例子幫我分一下嗎？

messages.short_answer: 依照論文的定義，冷卻時間和擊殺後拿金錢買裝備比較接近 Mechanics，因為它們是遊戲的規則與資源結構。玩家因此安排技能時機、決定買哪件裝備所形成的局勢起伏，比較接近 Dynamics；玩家看到裝備成形後的緊張或成就感，則屬於 Aesthetics。這是 PaperLens 依定義做的推論，論文本身並沒有討論《英雄聯盟》。

sections.title: 冷卻時間與買裝備屬於哪一層
sections.text: 冷卻時間、擊殺拿金錢、買裝備，都是事先寫進遊戲裡的規則與資源結構，因此可以歸為 Mechanics。論文說 Mechanics 是遊戲的「particular components」，也就是零件層級的東西。

sections.title: 哪些現象屬於 Dynamics
sections.text: 當玩家根據冷卻時間決定什麼時候開技能、或依金錢和隊友與對手的狀況決定買什麼，這些行為會隨著比賽時間反覆出現，形成局勢的起伏。這比較接近論文說的在執行時受玩家輸入與彼此輸出影響、隨時間產生的行為。

sections.title: 哪些感受屬於 Aesthetics
sections.text: 看到自己的裝備成形後的成就感，或在冷卻結束前後的緊張感，是玩家與系統互動時產生的情感反應，比較接近 Aesthetics。同一個冷卻規則，可能帶來緊張，也可能帶來放鬆，所以 Aesthetics 是玩家的感受而不是規則本身。

sections.title: 論文原文的類比與限制
sections.text: 論文在卡牌遊戲的例子中，把洗牌、吃牌、下注等規則稱為 Mechanics，把虛張聲勢這類行為稱為從這些規則中「emerge」出來的 Dynamics。這可以幫助你理解分層方式，但《英雄聯盟》的具體分類仍是 PaperLens 的推論，論文沒有直接處理，也可能因討論的角度不同而有不同分法。

sources.text: These pages introduce the MDA framework (Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics) for analysing and designing games, contrasting games with other entertainment products because their consumption is unpredictable. The framework treats games as artifacts whose content is their behavior, and defines Mechanics as data representations and algorithms, Dynamics as run-time behavior, and Aesthetics as desired emotional responses. Each component is presented as a lens causally linked to the others, with designer and player perspectives explained and experience-driven design favored over feature-driven design. The pages then move to a taxonomy of eight aesthetic categories (Sensation, Fantasy, Narrative, Challenge, Fellowship, Discovery, Expression, Submission), illustrated with examples of Charades, Quake, The Sims and Final Fantasy, and note there is no formula for what produces fun.

These pages introduce a taxonomy-based approach to describing games, using aesthetics, dynamics, and mechanics as a framework for understanding player appeal. They present aesthetic models, illustrated with competitive games like Charades and Quake, which rely on adversarial play and clear feedback about who is winning. The dynamics section explains how elements such as time pressure, information sharing, item building, and rising tension produce experiences like challenge, fellowship, expression, and dramatic tension. Using Monopoly as the main example, the pages describe how feedback loops can widen gaps between players and erode engagement, and suggest design fixes such as catch-up rewards. The pages do not state formal limitations beyond noting that realism may conflict with fun.

These pages discuss how game designers can adjust game mechanics to shape overall dynamics, using Monopoly as a running example: adding subsidies and taxes to keep lagging players competitive, adding time-pressure mechanics such as constant-rate taxes or doubled payouts, and iteratively play-testing and tuning values until the game is balanced. They note that aesthetic vocabulary and dynamic models (such as the D6 model for board size) help designers articulate goals, diagnose problems, and measure progress. The pages then argue that AI components cannot be treated as black boxes and must be evaluated for their effects on system behavior and player experience. Using a baby-sitting tag game prototyped across three passes (for 3-7 year-olds, for 7-12 year-old girls with a Rugrats-style franchise, and as a strategic military simulation for 14-35 year old men), the pages show how target audience and aesthetic goals change design requirements for dynamics, hiding places, and character behaviour.

For example, consider the games Charades, Quake, The Sims and Final Fantasy. While each are “fun” in their own right, it is much more informative to consider the aesthetic components that create their respective player experiences:

Charades: Fellowship, Expression, Challenge. Quake: Challenge, Sensation, Competition, Fantasy. The Sims: Discovery, Fantasy, Expression, Narrative. Final Fantasy: Fantasy, Narrative, Expression, Discovery, Challenge, Submission.

In this paper we present the MDA framework (standing for Mechanics, Dynamics, and Aesthetics), developed and taught as part of the Game Design and Tuning Workshop at the Game Developers Conference, San Jose 2001-2004 [LeBlanc, 2004a]. MDA is a formal approach to understanding games – one which attempts to bridge the gap between game design and development, game criticism, and technical game research. We believe this methodology will clarify and strengthen the iterative processes of developers, scholars and researchers alike, making it easier for all parties to decompose, study and design a broad class of game designs and game artifacts. Towards a Comprehensive Framework Game design and authorship happen at many levels, and the fields of games research and development involve people from diverse creative and scholarly backgrounds. While it’s often necessary to focus on one area, everyone, regardless of discipline, will at some point need to consider issues outside that area: base mechanisms of game systems, the overarching design goals, or the desired experiential results of gameplay.

Agents in this space, in addition to coordinating movement and attacks must operate over a wide range of sensory data. Reasoning about the pl ayer’s position and intent should indicate challenge, but promote their overall success. Will enemies be able to pass over obstacles and navigate challenging terrain, or will you “cheat”? Will sound propagation be “realistic” or will simple metrics based on distance suffice? Wrapping Up Here we see that simple changes in the aesthetic requirements of a game will introduce mechanical changes for its AI on many levels – sometimes requiring the development of entirely new systems for navigation, reasoning, and strategic problem solving.

Conversely, we see that there are no “AI mechanics” as such – intelligence or coherence comes from the interaction of AI logic with gameplay logic. Using the MDA framework, we can reason explicitly about aesthetic goals, draw out dynamics that support those goals, and then scope the range of our mechanics accordingly. Conclusions

Here we see that each game pursues multiple aesthetic goals, in varying degrees. Charades emphasizes Fellowship over Challenge; Quake provides Challenge as a main element of gameplay. And while there is no Grand Unified Theory of games or formula that details the combination and proportion of elements that will result in “fun”, this M D A Designer Player The designer and player each have a different perspective.

5. Fellowship Game as social framework 6. Discovery Game as uncharted territory 7. Expression Game as self-discovery 8. Submission Game as pastime Rules “Fun” System

Dynamics

For example, the mechanics of card games include shuffling, trick-taking and betting – from which dynamics like bluffing can emerge. The mechanics of shooters include weapons, ammunition and spawn points – which sometimes produce things like camping and sniping. The mechanics of golf include balls, clubs, sand traps and water hazards – which sometimes produce broken or drowned clubs.

Adjusting the mechanics of a game helps us fine-tune the game’s overall dynamics. Consider our Monopoly example. Mechanics that would help lagging players could include bonuses or “subsidies” for poor players, and penalties or “taxes” for rich players – perhaps calculated when crossing the Go square, leaving jail, or exercising monopolies over a certain threshold in value. By applying such changes to the fundamental rules of play, we might be able to keep lagging players competitive and interested for longer periods of time.

persona_text:
# Persona: Mei

**Who.** Mei is a third-year undergraduate from Taiwan taking a game design course, and a non-native
English speaker. A topic from the lecture caught her interest, so she is reading the teacher's extra
readings on her own.

**What she wants.** To understand the main ideas well enough to explain them and connect them to the
lecture. She has no research project. Reading goal: *Get a general overview of this paper*.

**How she behaves.**
- Writes in Traditional Chinese (繁體字). Interface language: 中文（繁體）.
- Has limited background. Starts with broad questions ("這篇在講什麼？"), then asks for basic definitions.
- Often restates an idea in her own words to check her understanding, and is sometimes wrong (e.g. mixes up
  mechanics and dynamics, or treats a game mechanic as the same thing as a rule or a goal).
- Says plainly when she still does not understand ("還是不太懂", "可以換個方式解釋嗎？").
- Tends to accept answers and rarely opens the sources unless prompted.
- Brings in examples from games she plays or from the lecture and asks whether they fit the paper.

**Papers.** MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research; Game Studies – Defining Game Mechanics.
